h1: The 4 Best Toaster Ovens Under $50 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Toaster Ovens Under $50: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: four toaster ovens that stay under $50, compared on slice capacity, interior volume, wattage and counter footprint.
summary: The Elite Gourmet ETO449X is our top pick for its 4-slice capacity, 800W element and pizza function. The ETO490 offers the biggest listed interior at 9L, the Dash Mini is the cheapest, and the ETO236 suits the tightest counters.
intro: A cheap toaster oven fails in a predictable way: buyers pick on slice count alone and then discover that a 2-slice oven will not take the pan they actually own. Under $50 the real choice is between size, wattage and a few convenience features, not brand prestige.

We reviewed the models whose price bucket sits entirely under $50 and ranked them on the spec sheet: capacity, interior volume, wattage and extras. Only four qualified, and we left out the pricier ovens even when they looked tempting.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ETO449X Toaster Oven
products.verdict: The most complete spec sheet under $50.
products.description:
The ETO449X is a 4-slice toaster oven with an 800W element, an 8.99L interior and a pizza function. It sits in the $25-50 bucket, so it stays within the limit.

Top spot goes to the oven whose listing names capacity, wattage, volume and a pizza setting all at once. The ETO490 below lists a slightly larger 9L interior, but without the wattage or pizza detail.

Buy it if you want one small oven to handle toast and the occasional frozen pizza. The caveat is that the listing gives few other details, so check the interior against your pan before ordering.
products.idealFor: Small households wanting toast and frozen pizza.
products.skipIf: You need a large pan or convection.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ETO490 9L/4-Slice Oven
products.verdict: A 9L, 4-slice oven aimed at busier households.
products.description:
The ETO490 lists a 4-slice capacity and a 9L interior. It sits in the $25-50 bucket, so it fits the budget.

It ranks just below the ETO449X because its listing does not name a wattage or a pizza setting, though its 9L interior is marginally larger. That is the only real spec gap between the two.

It suits busier households with heavier daily use, which is how the maker positions it. The caveat is the thin spec sheet, so confirm the wattage on the listing before you buy.
products.skipIf: You want a listed wattage or pizza mode.

products.name: Dash Mini Toaster Oven
products.verdict: The least expensive oven here, with a pizza function.
products.description:
The Dash Mini is a compact toaster oven with a pizza function, and it is the only pick in the under $25 bucket.

It ranks third because it lists no slice capacity or wattage, unlike the Elite Gourmet models above. In return it costs the least, which is the whole tradeoff.

It suits a first apartment or dorm shelf where price is the priority. The caveat is that the spec sheet is short, so check the listed interior size for your needs.
products.idealFor: Dorm rooms and first apartments on a tight budget.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ETO236 Compact 2-Slice Toaster Oven
products.verdict: A 2-slice oven for counters with no room to spare.
products.description:
The ETO236 is a compact 2-slice toaster oven in the $25-50 bucket.

It ranks last because two slices is the smallest capacity here and the listing names no wattage or extras. What you gain over the 4-slice models is a smaller footprint.

It suits limited space and solo cooks. The caveat is that a 2-slice oven will not hold larger pans, so skip it if you cook for more than one or two people.
products.idealFor: Solo cooks with very limited counter space.

whatMatters.detail: Slice count is the maker's shorthand for interior width. A 4-slice oven handles more bread or a small tray, while a 2-slice oven is easier to store. Check the listing for both slice count and interior volume rather than relying on one.
Volume in liters shows how much food fits at once. The ETO490 lists 9L and the ETO449X lists 8.99L, which is close. Look for the figure in the bullet points and compare it with the pan you own.
Wattage shows how much heating power the element has, which affects how quickly it preheats. Only the ETO449X lists 800W here. Look for it in the specs before assuming performance.
A pizza setting adapts the heating for frozen pizza. Both the Dash Mini and the ETO449X list one. Check the listing wording rather than assuming a dial label.
A toaster oven takes counter space and needs clearance. The 2-slice ETO236 is the smallest here. Measure your counter and compare it with the listed dimensions.

faq.q: Will a 4-slice oven fit a full-size pizza?
faq.a: No spec in the listings says so. The ETO449X lists a pizza function and an 8.99L interior, so expect smaller frozen pizzas and confirm dimensions first.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake?
faq.a: Buying on slice count alone. Compare interior volume as well, since the ETO490 lists 9L and the ETO449X lists 8.99L.

faq.q: Is a pricier oven worth it?
faq.a: If you want convection or air frying, yes, but those models sit above $50. For basic toasting, the ovens here are enough.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Place it on a flat counter with clearance around the sides and top. Read the manual for the pizza function if your model has one.

faq.q: How do I clean a small toaster oven?
faq.a: Unplug it, let it cool, and wipe the interior and crumbs out of the tray. Check the manual for removable parts.
None of the four lists convection. The convection models in the facts sit above $50.

finalTake: The Elite Gourmet ETO449X gives the most complete spec sheet under $50, and the ETO490 is the pick if interior volume matters more. The Dash Mini is the cheapest way to get a pizza function, and the ETO236 is for the tightest counters. Check your pan against the listed volume before ordering.
